reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive 46,XY disorder of sex development caused by mutations in SRD5A2
The enzyme converts testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone, which drives external genital virilisation
Affected 46,XY newborns typically have undervirilised or ambiguous external genitalia despite normal testes
Wolffian-derived internal structures are usually formed because they depend on testosterone rather than dihydrotestosterone
Marked virilisation often occurs at puberty as testosterone levels rise, sometimes prompting a change in perceived sex
An elevated ratio of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, especially after stimulation, supports the diagnosis
Prostate development and typical male-pattern balding are reduced because these are dihydrotestosterone dependent
reference.pathophysiology: Dihydrotestosterone is the principal androgen responsible for masculinising the external genitalia and prostate during fetal development, and it is produced from testosterone by the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase type 2. In SRD5A2 deficiency, reduced enzyme activity limits dihydrotestosterone formation, so the external genitalia of a 46,XY fetus are incompletely virilised even though testes and testosterone are present. Testosterone-dependent Wolffian structures develop, and anti-Mullerian hormone still causes Mullerian regression. At puberty the surge in testosterone can partially overcome the deficiency and produce substantial virilisation.
additionalInvestigations: Baseline and stimulated testosterone and dihydrotestosterone with calculation of their ratio
Anti-Mullerian hormone and gonadotropins to assess testicular function
Pelvic and genital imaging to define internal anatomy and gonadal position
redFlags: Ambiguous genitalia in a newborn requiring urgent multidisciplinary assessment
Rapid virilisation at puberty causing distress or prompting reconsideration of sex of rearing
Undescended or intra-abdominal gonads needing evaluation and monitoring
Diagnostic uncertainty that risks incorrect early sex assignment
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable with multidisciplinary care; fertility may be possible in some individuals, and management, including any decisions about hormone therapy or surgery, should be individualised and guided by the person's gender identity.
pitfalls: Confusing the condition with partial androgen insensitivity without measuring the testosterone to dihydrotestosterone ratio
Making irreversible early decisions about sex of rearing before the diagnosis is clarified
Underestimating the degree of virilisation that can occur at puberty
Neglecting psychological support during evaluation and management
